W7222492951.abstract: Abstract Multi‐agent artificial intelligence (MAAI) systems are increasingly deployed across economic and digital infrastructures. Existing regulatory frameworks, including the EU AI Act and related initiatives, largely focus on individual AI systems and are therefore poorly suited to govern risks that arise from agent interaction. This paper argues that multi‐agent AI introduces distinct governance challenges, including emergent behavior, tacit coordination, cascading systemic risks, and difficulties in assigning accountability. Traditional risk management approaches, which rely on static and component‐based analysis, are inadequate for adaptive, networked systems operating across jurisdictions. Through a comparative review of policy developments in the European Union, United States, and Asia‐Pacific region, the paper identifies a growing governance gap, alongside early regulatory experimentation such as China's emerging standards for intelligent agents. The paper concludes that effective oversight will require a shift from model‐centric regulation toward system‐level and adaptive governance frameworks capable of addressing the collective dynamics of multi‐agent AI systems.

W7222918358.abstract: Text classification is a widely studied problem in information retrieval and data mining, with applications ranging from healthcare diagnosis to the detection of COVID-19-related fake news. Social media platforms generate vast volumes of user-generated text, and the rapid spread of misinformation during the pandemic has made automated fake news detection an important task. In this study, we apply pretrained transformer-based transfer learning (TL) models and large language models (LLMs), namely BERT-base, ALBERT-base, XLM-RoBERTa-base, DistilBERT, GPT-2, XLNet, and T5, to the COVID-19 English Tweets dataset, which contains 6,420 tweets labeled as real or fake. To further improve performance, we apply six late-fusion optimization techniques: weighted fusion, particle swarm optimization (PSO) fusion, the Nelder-Mead algorithm, Powell's method, the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) algorithm, and trust-region constrained optimization. Models are evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, and confusion-matrix heatmaps are used to visualize the predictions of each model. GPT-2 achieved the best performance, with an accuracy of 0.9631, precision of 0.9612, recall of 0.9610, and F1-score of 0.9600, while Nelder-Mead fusion achieved the best result among the fusion methods with an accuracy of 0.9610. These results highlight the value of LLMs for COVID-19 fake news detection. We conclude by outlining future directions, including multiclass classification, multilingual datasets, and real-time social media streams.

W7223052750.abstract: Looped large language models trade parameter storage for recurrent computation, but most are trained from scratch. In practice, pretraining with looped depth is expensive, making post-training upcycling of a pretrained non-looped LLM an attractive alternative. We introduce \textbf{UpLoop}, a post-training recipe based on \emph{layer-wise} recurrence. Instead of looping a whole model or a middle block, UpLoop loops each selected layer locally, preserving the pretrained depth hierarchy and avoiding feature-space mismatch. To make loop execution useful, we add hidden-wise gates on the attention and MLP residual branches, so later loops act as progressive refinements rather than redundant rewrites. Empirically, UpLoop breaks the commonly observed saturation at two loops ($R=2$) in prior looped models. Starting from Qwen3-4B Base and applying SFT, UpLoop improves the average accuracy across 20 benchmarks by 6.17\% at $R=3$. We use $R=3$ as the main setting for the best accuracy--cost trade-off, while both native and extrapolated $R=4$ yield further gains.

W7223143244.abstract: The goal of phishing attacks, which rank high among cyber risks, is to steal sensitive information (such as login passwords, financial data, and more) from unsuspecting people and companies. Blacklist, whitelist, rule, heuristic, and signature-based detection methods are no longer suitable due to the rising sophistication of phishing schemes. As a result, ML, DL, and NLP are rapidly becoming into effective instruments for detecting both well-known and brand-new forms of phishing. Background on phishing assaults, old ways of detecting them, and recent advances in intelligent phishing detection are all included in this article. It delves into several machine learning algorithms such as decision tree, LSTM, ANN, CNN, and RNN, as well as deep learning models like KNN, NB, and SVM. Also, natural language processing methods including word embedding, sentiment analysis, text categorization, and tokenization are explored with the aim of detecting phishing material. Presenting a comprehensive, precise, and up-to-the-minute phishing detection system is the ultimate goal of this study, which focuses on machine learning frameworks, performance indicators, present obstacles, and future research directions.

W7223178158.abstract: Introduction: Minimally invasive surgery (MIS), including endovascular and robot-assisted procedures, is widely used for vascular pathologies but remains limited by technical complexity, cognitive workload, and postoperative complications. Artificial Intelligence (AI) may help address these challenges through predictive analysis, decision support, image analysis, and automation. Methods: A structured Google Scholar search was conducted from February 21, 2025, to January 1, 2026, and updated through September 2026. Peer-reviewed studies applying AI to vascular MIS were included, with additional targeted searches addressing clinical translation, deployment, regulation, and ethical considerations. Results: Thirty primary studies were analyzed, including eight on machine learning, nine on deep learning, four on natural language processing, and nine on robotics or reinforcement learning. Machine learning supported risk stratification and outcome prediction, deep learning enabled imaging and segmentation applications, natural language processing facilitated clinical information extraction, and robotic systems supported navigation and procedural assistance. Discussion: AI demonstrates substantial potential across the vascular MIS pathway, but broader clinical adoption requires stronger validation, prospective multicenter studies, standardized reporting, health-economic evaluation, and careful consideration of regulatory, liability, and accessibility challenges.

W7223244744.abstract: In response to vast and widespread online tracking, regulators and technologists alike have worked to develop laws and tools that allow people to express their privacy preferences. These measures seek to offer users greater control over the sale and sharing of personal information, putting agency in their hands to protect their privacy. However, the web is undergoing a seismic shift, away from strictly user-driven behavior towards agentic behavior, where AI agents take autonomous actions on behalf of users. In this study, we ask: What should privacy preference controls look like in the agentic web and agentic systems more generally? To answer this question, we develop a taxonomy of enforceable privacy preferences for agentic systems. Our taxonomy is informed both by laws and empirical studies of existing privacy tools as well as an audit of 30 leading AI assistants and agent platforms. To explore how our taxonomy can be implemented, we design and develop eight open-source prototypes that mirror real-world agentic applications and demonstrate how major aspects of our taxonomy can be structurally integrated in agentic protocols, such as the Model Control Protocol and Agent2Agent protocol. Ultimately, our study seeks to provide the groundwork for ensuring end-user privacy and autonomy is not lost in the newly arriving agentic world.

W7223288806.abstract: Language-model agents acquire capability along two routes that published work almost always varies together, one enlarging the computation a single agent performs and the other enlarging the number of agents and the channels along which they pass partial results, which leaves the contribution of each route indistinguishable. This paper separates an agent system into a reasoning operator and an interaction topology, holding the number of agents fixed at three across all multi-agent topologies, together with the number of rounds, the message cap, the prompt skeleton, and the memory settings for all combinations, and evaluates a full factorial design of four reasoning levels and four topologies on three public test sets totalling 484 instances under five random seeds, giving 38,720 task executions. Comparisons are paired at the instance level, and effects are estimated from logistic mixed-effects models fitted to each test set separately. The reasoning factor spans 18.0 points on the static suite whereas the topology factor spans 7.8 points on the interactive one, a reversal indicating that the two mechanisms act on different failure modes. The topology span is taken across all four topology levels and therefore includes the step from one agent to three, against a structure-only span of 2.8 points among the multi-agent topologies. The two factors also depart from additivity in a localised manner. A mechanism-motivated single-degree-of-freedom contrast on the only cell in which both factors contribute a corrective pass is significant at p = 0.001 on the static suite, whereas the omnibus nine-degree-of-freedom interaction test is not (p = 0.094), and in that cell the observed 50.0 percent lies 5.8 points below the additive expectation. After tokens are counted, seven of the sixteen configurations remain undominated on the static suite and five on the operating-system suite, and returns saturate at 12,400 tokens per instance on the static suite under the present design.

W7223337719.abstract: Many recent open-weight language models use n-gram embedding tables to improve performance. These tables store learned representations of short token sequences, such as pairs or triples of consecutive tokens, which the model retrieves during processing. However, they can require substantial memory: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, for example, allocates 196 billion parameters to its Engram n-gram memory. We therefore investigate whether this memory cost can be reduced while preserving the performance improvement that the tables provide. We propose storing n-gram embeddings at low precision and systematically investigate different quantization methods and bit allocations across tables. Across nanochat-, Llama-, and GPT-2-family models trained from scratch, four-bit tables save approximately 75% of table memory while preserving more than 99% of the validation-loss improvement from adding the tables. Using fewer bits leads to a larger drop in performance, although we find that a short fine-tuning phase recovers a significant part of this loss. In addition, reinvesting the saved memory in larger tables can improve performance beyond that of the original full-precision tables while still using less memory. These table memory savings also extend to large existing models: on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, low-bit tables save 47-55% of table memory, with perplexity increases of less than 1.2% and largely preserved downstream task performance. These findings establish low-bit precision as a practical way to reduce the memory requirements of n-gram embeddings and use the saved capacity to improve model performance.

W7223341025.abstract: Recent reports, such as "Who is using AI to code?", indicate that approximately 30\% of Python code contributions to GitHub are AI-generated. Given the inherent unreliability of this code, formal verification emerges as a promising approach to establish trust in software correctness. Although leveraging large language models (LLMs) for formal verification has garnered increasing attention, practical adoption remains limited due to the challenges in writing formal specifications and verifying program correctness against them. Existing tools predominantly support verification for languages such as Java and C, with minimal support for Python. We present TrustedCode, an automated framework for verifying AI-generated Python code. TrustedCode uses LLMs to (i) type-check Python code, (ii) translate it into WhyML via the Why3 framework, and (iii) verify it against formal specifications using Why3 back-end automated theorem provers. Our method integrates chain-of-thought prompting through LangGraph to identify and address LLM limitations in specification generation and proving the specified programs. To evaluate TrustedCode, we conducted experiments on ten Python programs of varying complexity. Our analysis reveals that 50\% of the observed errors stem from domain knowledge gaps, 30\% from syntactic inaccuracies, and the remaining 20\% from semantic and type-related issues. These findings underscore the importance of targeted improvements in LLM-guided formal verification workflows for Python. TrustedCode is an open source tool available at: \href{github.com/mtaimoorkhan/TrustedCode}{github.com/mtaimoorkhan/TrustedCode}. The video demonstration is available at: \href{youtu.be/Nr5I2g8ec-s}{youtu.be/Nr5I2g8ec-s}

W7223655043.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly capable of supporting scientific workflows, but their capabilities across diverse research activities remain difficult to assess systematically. Existing benchmarks often focus on selected scientific capabilities or task types, limiting a comprehensive characterization of scientific agents' strengths and weaknesses in realistic research workflows. We introduce SCI-AGENT-EXAM, a workflow-oriented benchmark comprising 120 expert-curated tasks across 11 scientific fields and 7 research task types defined by the Scientific Workflow Task Taxonomy (SWTT). Each task requires both executable artifacts (e.g., code and scripts) and textual artifacts (e.g., reports and explanations). To evaluate the heterogeneous task outputs, we develop a hybrid evaluation protocol combining deterministic programmatic verification for executable artifacts with a calibrated, expert-validated LLM-based judge for textual artifacts. Beyond outcome assessment, we analyze progress and solution stability along execution trajectories to characterize how agents reach their final results. Experiments with 10 frontier LLM agents reveal substantial performance gaps: GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest overall score of 80.9, yet only 26.0% of its runs exceed the 0.95 success threshold. Further analyses uncover distinct capability profiles across scientific task types and substantial variation in execution efficiency and stability. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/SKYLENAGE-AI/Sci-Agent-Exam.

W7223665902.abstract: Feeding a pretrained language model the expected embedding of its own next-token distribution turns it into a discrete-time dynamical system with continuous states. Across Qwen2.5, OLMo-2 and Llama-3 models from 0.5B to 72B parameters, temperature and activation steering move this loop between repeating text and chaos, with positive finite-time Lyapunov exponents. The loop's derivative factorizes into the inverse temperature, the covariance of token embeddings under the next-token distribution (a cross-covariance for untied embeddings) and the network's Jacobian. In one model studied in detail, along recorded orbits, the growth that steering adds comes mainly from the readout, where next tokens compete. The periodic windows show the quantitative signatures of low-dimensional maps, from saddle-node scaling and Feigenbaum's constant to shrimp-shaped domains; passage times predicted in advance from the model's derivatives came within one return-map iterate of the measured passage times in 42 of 48 cases over two prospective stages (24 and 18 of 24), and interval arithmetic proves attracting periodic orbits of the full transformer map. Numerical reproducibility depends on the dynamical regime: changing only the batch layout changed the text of 173 of 192 chaotic float64 loops in the smallest model, compared with only 7 of 192 periodic ones. These results show that bifurcation theory can make quantitative predictions about continuous language-model feedback, with rigorous guarantees for selected periodic orbits of the full transformer.

W7223786905.abstract: Hydrogen has become a pivotal component in the global pursuit of carbon neutral and sustainable energy systems owing to its high-gravimetric energy density, fuel flexibility, and cross sectoral applicability. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of contemporary hydrogen technologies encompassing production, storage, and utilization, with an emphasis on their scientific principles, material innovations, and engineering challenges. Major production pathways, including water electrolysis, thermochemical and photoelectrochemical splitting, biomass derived routes, and emerging solar-driven hybrid methods, are critically evaluated with respect to energy efficiency, techno economic trends, and integration potential with renewable resources. Advances in hydrogen storage are examined across compressed, liquefied, and solid state systems, highlighting progress in metal hydrides, carbon-based porous media, and nanostructured materials that promise enhanced safety, reversibility, and storage density. Utilization technologies such as proton exchange membrane (PEM) and solid oxide fuel cells, direct hydrogen combustion systems, and hybrid power modules are reviewed with attention to catalytic performance, thermal stability, degradation pathways, and system level optimization. Additionally, cross cutting issues including lifecycle emissions, infrastructure readiness, safety protocols, and the role of hydrogen in sector coupling are assessed to outline broader deployment challenges. The review concludes by identifying future research opportunities in advanced materials design, artificial intelligence enabled process optimization, and circular economy strategies aimed at accelerating hydrogen's role as a foundational pillar of next generation clean energy systems. Representative hydrogen production technologies exhibit efficiencies ranging from ∼60%–85% for water electrolysis, hydrogen purity above 99.9% for PEM electrolysis, and production costs that typically range from about USD 3–8 kg−1 for green hydrogen depending on electricity price and technology. These comparisons indicate that while green hydrogen offers superior environmental performance, further improvements in efficiency, cost reduction, and technology maturity are required for widespread commercialization.

W7223802411.abstract: Despite rapid progress in evaluating large language models, the Lost in the Middle phenomenon - a persistent weakness of Transformer-based models whereby information near the middle of the context window exerts less influence on generation - remains unresolved. This paper examines the phenomenon in Serbian, among the first such studies outside English, evaluating three recent open-weight small language models on a filtered multi-document QA dataset. Each query contains a question and ten documents, only one of which holds the answer; its position is shifted from first to tenth place to measure the resulting change in accuracy. A dedicated evaluation procedure was developed to account for the morphological complexity of Serbian, combining string-based matching with a final LLM-based judgment stage (Claude Haiku) for cases obscured by grammatical case variation. Within this dataset and context length, a Cochran's Q test revealed no statistically significant accuracy degradation for any of the three models as the gold document approached the middle of the context. Larger differences were instead observed between the models: Gemma-4-26B-A4B (92.9%) and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (91.9%) could not be distinguished statistically (p = 0.151), while GPT-OSS-20B (87.3%) was reliably weaker than both (p < 0.0001), suggesting that model choice may play a more important role than gold-document position.

W7223835807.abstract: Memory has become a central mechanism for extending large language models (LLMs) beyond fixed context windows, stateless interaction, and static parametric knowledge. This survey organizes the literature around three complementary dimensions: the life cycle of memory, the storage substrate, and the system role that memory plays in LLM-based agents, while using cognitive-science-inspired memory concepts as a lightweight conceptual motivation rather than as a separate technical contribution or implementation family. On this basis, we distinguish three mechanism families: nonparametric memory, where information is stored outside model parameters in text, graph, multimodal, or database-like structures; parametric memory, where information is stored or accessed through activations, key-value caches, learned modules, adapter-based parameterizations, or model weights; and memory for agent evolution, where stored experiences support reinforcement learning, continual learning, procedural reuse, context engineering, and agent harness design. Evaluation is treated as a separate cross-cutting component rather than as a memory mechanism. Unlike surveys that focus primarily on retrieval-augmented generation or long-context modeling, this paper emphasizes the full memory life cycle: construction, maintenance, retrieval, consolidation, forgetting, governance, and evaluation. By aligning conceptual motivations, computational memory mechanisms, benchmarks, and deployment concerns, the survey provides a structured roadmap for designing memory-augmented LLM agents that are persistent, adaptive, auditable, and safe to update over time.

W7224002213.abstract: Enterprise workflow automation has progressed from rigid, rule-based Robotic Process Automation (RPA) toward cognitive systems capable of perception, reasoning, and autonomous action. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in natural language understanding and generation, single-model deployments remain limited in multi-step planning, long-horizon memory, tool orchestration, and verifiable decision-making, which are essential for real-world enterprise workflows. This paper introduces AIWA-Agent, an Intelligent Multi-Agent Workflow Automation Framework that integrates a Planning Agent, a Reasoning Agent, a Memory Agent, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) module, a Tool-Calling Agent, an Execution Agent, and a Validation Agent under a Human-in-the-Loop and Explainable AI (XAI) supervision layer. Unlike prior single-agent LLM assistants and loosely coupled multi-agent toolkits, AIWA-Agent formalizes agent interaction through seven governing mathematical constructs Workflow Automation Efficiency , Agent Collaboration Score , Task Completion Accuracy, Workflow Latency , Resource Utilization , LLM Confidence Score , and Agent Decision Score enabling quantitative, explainable orchestration rather than ad hoc prompt chaining. We formalize the framework's architecture, mathematical model, and methodology, and evaluate it through a structured experimental protocol comparing AIWA-Agent against Catgut (single-agent), Autopsy, Crewel, Lang Graph, and Autopen baselines using illustrative, internally consistent performance data across accuracy, latency, collaboration, and resource metrics, together with descriptive statistics, correlation, regression, ANOVA, and reliability analysis. Results indicate that the proposed coordination and validation layers yield measurable gains in workflow efficiency and task success while preserving interpretability. The findings offer a reproducible blueprint for enterprises pursuing agented automation with governance and explain ability by design.

W7224114274.abstract: In recent years, multi-agent systems have shifted from rule-based, symbolic agents to sub-symbolic agents built on language models. However, several limitations remain unresolved. The new frontier is neuro-symbolic agents, which pair language models with deterministic tools and explicit protocols. Without a common framework to standardize and compose them, each study rebuilds the same infrastructure, and results are hard to replicate. This paper presents EREBOTS 4.0, an open-source, hybrid-AI, multi-agent framework that fills this gap for conversational assistants. Language-model agents plan and route requests, while deterministic tools compute exact results over the Model Context Protocol (MCP). An orchestrator selects one or more specialist agents per turn and calls them over the Agent2Agent protocol (A2A). A new agent, local or remote, is added by listing its URL in a configuration file. The framework also manages identity, user context with consent flags, task states and traces. Its A2A server passed 97 tracked requirements in the official A2A Technology Compatibility Kit, with no failures.

W7224137183.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), encompassing Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, remains a complex and heterogeneous condition with variable response to biologic therapies. Despite significant advances with anti-TNF agents, integrin inhibitors, and interleukin-12/23 blockers, treatment outcomes are limited by primary nonresponse, secondary loss of efficacy, immunogenicity, and substantial healthcare costs. The advent of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms, offers new opportunities to address these challenges by integrating diverse clinical, laboratory, imaging, histologic, genetic, and microbiome data. Recent studies demonstrate that AI-based models achieve high accuracy in predicting biologic response, remission, and adverse outcomes, outperforming conventional statistical approaches. AI has also shown promise in real-time endoscopic assessment, histologic grading, and forecasting disease progression, enabling earlier intervention and personalized therapy. However, current models are constrained by limited datasets, heterogeneity, lack of large-scale prospective validation, and concerns regarding interpretability, transparency, and patient privacy. Future efforts should prioritize multicenter trials, external validation, and ethical integration into clinical workflows. Collectively, AI-driven prediction of biologic therapy response represents a pivotal step toward precision medicine in IBD, with the potential to optimize therapeutic strategies, reduce ineffective treatment exposure, and improve patient outcomes.

W7224222202.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) encode vast amounts of knowledge in their parameters, but these facts often require precise post-training rectification as they become outdated or incorrect over time.Traditional batch editing methods typically apply a uniform update strength across all instances.However, this uniform approach ignores the inherent variation in editing difficulty, leading to a fundamental tradeoff between correction success and model stability.To overcome this limitation, we introduce AdaPE (Adaptive Pressure Editing), a parameter-free adaptive editing framework that dynamically adjusts the update behavior for each specific instance.Specifically, we derive a closed-form adaptive update rate based on the ratio of residual energy to spatial sensitivity, which strictly quantifies the intrinsic injection difficulty.This formulation adaptively limits the update strength for difficult facts to preserve model locality, while ensuring sufficient knowledge injection for easier ones.Extensive experiments on three benchmarks and two prominent LLMs demonstrate the superiority of our approach in consistently circumventing the fixedstrength bottleneck, achieving a new state-ofthe-art balance between editing efficacy and model integrity.Our code is available at https: //github.com/skyandkibo/adape.

W7224300173.abstract: Compact open-source language models lag behind their larger counterparts in agentic tooluse reliability, yet standard remedies face fundamental obstacles: supervised fine-tuning suffers from exposure bias, while reinforcement learning is hampered by sparse credit assignment over long tool-interaction trajectories.We introduce Skill-CDPO, a progressive framework that first acquires tooluse skills at inference time through static tool analysis and dynamic strategy refinement, then distills the resulting error-correction signals into parameter updates via Critical Step DPO (CDPO).CDPO identifies the specific trajectory steps where model capability is the bottleneck-through rollout divergence between a local policy and an expert modeland constructs distributional preference pairs from all cross-group rollouts at those steps, weighted by both step-level criticality and pair-level score gaps.This provides dense, fine-grained supervision without requiring a process reward model.We evaluate Skill-CDPO on three medical agent benchmarks-PubMed Search (a new PubMed-based deep research benchmark we contribute), CURE-Bench, and MedBrowseComp-using an 8Bparameter deep research model.Skill-CDPO substantially outperforms SFT and trajectorylevel DPO baselines and achieves competitive or superior performance compared to GPT-5.2 on retrieval-intensive tasks.Our code and data are available at https://github.com/ Adam135792468/CDPO. 1

W7224319160.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can match local semantic clues in knowledge graphs (KGs), but complex KGQA often requires satisfying the full dependency structure of a question.Existing retrieval-based methods therefore risk producing reasoning paths that look plausible at each step but violate the query's global intent.We propose Guiding Graph, a schema-light query-structure interface that turns KGQA from open-ended semantic traversal into structure-constrained query completion.A Guiding Graph exposes the entities, placeholders, and global dependencies that KG exploration must preserve, serving as an operational interface between natural language and graph traversal.The interface is training-free by default through prompt-based construction, and can optionally be strengthened with a cold-start fine-tuned constructor trained from limited bootstrapped supervision.Given the constructed Guiding Graph, exploration is governed by target selection from the query structure, structure-guided pruning before semantic matching, and target-scoped semantic alignment under the current Guiding Graph triple.Experiments on WebQSP, CWQ, and a domain-specific agricultural KG show that explicit query-structure guidance improves accuracy, robustness, and efficiency, with especially clear benefits for multi-hop reasoning and smaller LLMs.

W7224911845.abstract: Quantum materials exhibit diverse electronic and functional phenomena, but their characterization requires extensive experimental expertise, iterative decision-making and accumulated laboratory knowledge that is difficult to document and transfer. Here we introduce Quantum Agent (QUANTA), an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for autonomous quantum-materials characterization. Using a widely adopted Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS) as an experimental platform, QUANTA combines retrieval augmentation using scientific literature, experimental protocols and prior measurements with specialized agents for experimental planning, troubleshooting, and data interpretation. A separate deterministic control layer validates instrument actions. Guided by incoming data, QUANTA evaluates measurement quality, revises experimental plans and selects subsequent measurements. We demonstrate these capabilities through transport measurements of the topological Weyl semimetal TaP, as well as investigations of nonlinear responses in magnetic material Co2MnGa. These results establish QUANTA as a generalizable framework for evidence-driven, safeguarded and closed-loop quantum-materials characterization.

W7225075241.abstract: ABSTRACT Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) present new opportunities to advance text‐based analyses, particularly for identifying and disambiguating geospatial information expressed as natural language text. This study explores the capabilities of an LLM to identify, classify, and spatially query geospatial expressions found in urban planning documents. Urban planning encodes regulatory information, domain expertise, and local knowledge, much of which is geographic in nature, in reports and plans. Interpreting this geographic information is challenging for professionals (e.g., planners and lawyers) and community members. This paper presents an automated pipeline developed to assess an LLM's ability to extract geospatial expressions, determine their relevant spatial scale (micro, meso, and macro), and to identify urban features referenced by a specific development proposal. Three types of planning documents were examined from a mid‐sized city (Kitchener, Ontario, and Canada), namely a City‐authored Official Plan (OP), private consultants' development proposal reports, and transcripts from public meetings. A hierarchical Retrieval‐Augmented Generation (RAG) model processed text to extract explicit and implicit geospatial expressions, and a multi‐agent architecture converted these expressions into SQL queries against municipal data layers. Performance varied systematically by expression type and document type. The model handled implicit expressions best in the public‐meeting transcripts but performed poorly on explicit expressions in property‐specific reports. On a paired comparison, the pipeline outperformed two established geoparsing tools (GeospaCy and Mordecai3) on locally‐grounded planning documents. While this work illustrates how LLMs could automate interpretation of urban planning documents, the approach could also be applied to other application contexts where geospatial references are encoded in text forms.

W7225098775.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in finance has evolved from statistical learning and machine learning for structured prediction, through deep learning and foundation models for representation learning, language understanding, and reasoning, to retrieval-augmented generation for knowledge-grounded reasoning and agentic AI for autonomous planning and execution. In this paper, we examine how researchers and practitioners can select and apply AI methods in finance. We first show that the major paradigms of financial AI address fundamentally different classes of problems, rather than forming a strict hierarchy of capability. We then review the current state of research on AI in finance and trace how these paradigms have reshaped financial data, financial tasks, decision support, and human-AI collaboration. Building on this, we propose practical guidelines for matching AI paradigms to task characteristics, and show that more advanced models, such as foundation models or autonomous agents, are not universally superior. We conclude by outlining open challenges for researchers and practitioners working toward reliable financial AI.

W7225128819.abstract: Cardiorenal syndrome (CRS) encompasses a spectrum of disorders arising from bidirectional interactions between the heart and kidneys and is associated with substantial morbidity, mortality, and healthcare burden. Early recognition remains challenging because conventional biomarkers and imaging modalities may inadequately detect subclinical disease or distinguish functional changes from true organ injury. This narrative review examines the epidemiology, classification, pathophysiology, diagnostic approaches, and contemporary management of CRS, with particular emphasis on the emerging role of artificial intelligence (AI). Relevant evidence regarding established and emerging diagnostic and therapeutic approaches was reviewed, including biomarkers, imaging, guideline-directed medical therapy, ultrafiltration, cardiac devices, transplantation, and AI-based applications. Current evidence demonstrates the multifactorial nature of CRS and highlights the importance of early diagnosis and individualized management. Machine learning and deep learning approaches have shown potential to integrate electronic health records, biomarkers, imaging, physiological signals, and multi-omics data to support early detection, risk stratification, outcome prediction, and therapeutic decision-making. AI-assisted approaches may complement conventional diagnostic and management strategies and facilitate more precise and proactive CRS care. However, limitations related to data quality, model interpretability, external validation, and clinical implementation must be addressed before widespread clinical adoption.

W7225184045.abstract: The rise of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) in the built environment is shifting attention from isolated AI tools toward autonomous systems that reason, plan, and act across project and organizational workflows. The effectiveness of such systems depends not only on large language model capabilities, but also on the readiness of heterogeneous data environments across the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) sector. These environments combine structured sources, such as CAD and BIM models, schedules, cost databases, and asset registers, with unstructured ones, including technical reports, design narratives, planning and policy documents, contracts, meeting minutes, and risk registers. This paper reviews how built environment data can be organized to support agentic AI-ready workflows, focusing on knowledge structures, interoperability, and access and integration mechanisms such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Drawing on existing literature, it examines approaches proposed to organize structured and unstructured data and considers how such data can be contextualized and made accessible to AI agents in a reliable manner. The paper synthesizes current perspectives, highlights challenges around fragmentation and interoperability, and identifies open questions for future research on AI-compatible information management in the built environment.

W7225224277.abstract: The decline of brain functions due to the neurodegenerative process occurring over time with aging is often referred to as Alzheimer's Disease (AD). This gradual breakdown of brain tissue is responsible for the greater incidence of dementia and diminished capacity for thinking as adults age. The continued research in this field has been complicated by the fact that pathological changes in the brain frequently occur long before clinical symptoms are present. With advances in both AI and neuroimaging technology, there are promising possibilities for identifying disease-specific biomarkers for diagnosing AD at early asymptomatic stages. This review will provide a detailed overview of how AI and neuroimaging-based biomarkers are being integrated to diagnose AD as early as possible. The review assesses many types of biomarkers related to Alzheimer's Disease (AD) including genetic, molecular, Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF), blood, and digital biomarkers as well as their use in identifying pathological changes. Additionally, the review provides a description of important neuroimaging methods (MRI, PET, CT, and EEG) that contribute to obtaining structural and functional information about brain abnormalities associated with AD. Specific mention is made of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, convolutional neural networks, and predictive analytical models that allow for automatic extraction of features from large-scale medical data, identification of patterns, and classification of data. In addition to exploring the potential benefits of AI-based diagnostic tools for improving accuracy, shortening the time it takes to arrive at a diagnosis, and assisting in making clinical decisions, the review also highlights many of the potential obstacles to successful implementation of AI-driven diagnostic tools. Though there has been substantial evidence produced that supports the viability of these tools, a number of factors remain as substantial barriers to successful implementation: heterogeneous data sets; limited data availability; difficulties in interpretation; ethical issues; no standardized method of clinical validation. Moving forward, researchers will explore several possible solutions to these issues: integrating multiple types of data; developing explainable AI models; and creating individualized predictive models to provide better disease management. As a whole, the combination of artificial intelligence and neuroimaging offers an exciting potential to revolutionize the early detection and diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease, enabling timely intervention, enhanced patient outcomes, and improved treatment strategies.

W7225308881.abstract: Organizational decisions are linked to actions through autonomous AI agents which influence employees' work and operational delivery. The aim of this study is to propose an integrated framework for provenance in regulated enterprises across human resource management (HRM), labour management (LM), operations management (OM) and industrial relations (IR). The research is an integrative synthesis of 40 different research publications between 2001 and 2026 and descriptive secondary analysis of 20 publicly reported survey estimates. The literature is structured around four themes: Provenance and accountability, HR and organizational decisions, labor and industrial relations and human-AI operational performance. The synthesis sets out four interconnected requirements: the same context for both sources and execution, explicit delegation and human contribution, linkages between employment arrangements and operational delivery, and traceable participation and evaluation. These requirements are translated into eight proposed evidence dimensions that include mandate, rules, inputs, configuration, execution, participation, outcomes and stewardship. The differences in the shares reporting positive workforce and operational outcomes, based on public employer consultation data, range from 9.30 to 15.00 percentage points. Implementation context is provided by training, managerial decision and governance indicators. The main analytical result is the link between technical execution and institutional arrangements for people and work that is established through meaningful provenance. The study provides a 40-study evidence matrix, four research figures, a public data comparison that can be replicated, and seven proposed evaluation measures to help guide future workforce decisions and operational coordination and evaluate reconstruction quality in enterprises.

W7225428598.abstract: Abstract Efforts to reduce homogenization in large language model (LLM) outputs increasingly use prompting interventions, but these interventions often change both the information supplied to models and the instructions governing its use. We experimentally separate this behavioral guidance from a second potential source of variation: the information available during generation. Across 16,200 generations spanning three preregistered studies and two cross-model robustness replications, supplying heterogeneous external cues substantially increased semantic diversity and generally did so more reliably than explicit instructions to produce different responses. Crucially, this effect did not increase monotonically with stronger instructions to use the information. Merely presenting varied cues produced substantial diversification, whereas instructing models to disregard the same information largely eliminated the effect. When cue identities and cue-use instructions were held constant, differentiation instructions increased collective diversity relative to the other experimental conditions and increased departure from models’ default response spaces, whereas convergence instructions reduced such departure. These findings distinguish two sources of variation often conflated in prompt design: informational inputs can supply variation, while accompanying instructions can suppress their influence or further shape the resulting response distribution. Preserving diversity may therefore require designing information environments, not simply better prompts.
